historical_precedents.event: Philippines v. China Permanent Court of Arbitration case

Long-running territorial disputes in contested waters have historically constrained joint oil and gas exploration in the same areas, since companies are typically reluctant to invest amid unresolved sovereignty claims.

A manufacturer's inability to keep pace with demand for a breakout drug has historically triggered shortages, compounding-pharmacy workarounds, and counterfeit-product risk in the gap before supply catches up.

linked_playbooks.name: Pharmaceutical patent cliff and blockbuster drug revenue loss

A country crossing the 'super-aged society' threshold (21%+ population 65+) has historically required either new dedicated funding mechanisms, as with Japan's long-term-care insurance, or rising general healthcare spending as a share of GDP, or both.

Shipping insurers have historically raised war-risk premiums for vessels transiting the Gulf during periods of heightened tension, adding to the landed cost of oil and other cargo.

ripple_effect.name: Low-cost carriers disrupt legacy airline pricing after deregulation

historical_precedents.event: Ryanair adopts the low-cost carrier model as EU aviation deregulation takes effect
historical_precedents.what_happened: Ryanair restructured itself into a low-cost carrier starting in 1990, after its founders studied Southwest Airlines' model in the United States; the airline standardized on an all-Boeing 737 fleet and cut its cheapest return fare from £99 to £59. When Ryanair had launched its Dublin-London Luton route in 1987 under partial EEC air-travel deregulation, it priced return fares at £99 — roughly half the prevailing legacy-carrier rate — prompting Aer Lingus and British Airways to cut their own fares to £95 and £94.99 in response. The EU's Single Aviation Market, established in 1992, and further deregulation in April 1997 removed remaining cabotage restrictions and enabled Ryanair's rapid pan-European expansion, with annual passengers growing from about 745,000 in 1990 to 66.5 million by 2010.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Ryanair's model was subsequently adopted by other low-cost carriers including easyJet, WestJet, and AirAsia, restructuring competitive pricing across the European aviation market over the following decades.

historical_precedents.event: US Airline Deregulation Act and the growth of low-cost, point-to-point carriers
historical_precedents.what_happened: Following the 1978 US Airline Deregulation Act, low-cost carriers such as Southwest Airlines expanded point-to-point service that competed directly with legacy hub-and-spoke carriers on price.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Average US fares per passenger mile fell about 9% between 1979 and 1994, and inflation-adjusted fares fell roughly 30% between 1976 and 1990; a New York-Los Angeles round trip that would have cost an inflation-adjusted $1,442 in 1974 could be purchased for around $268 by 2010, though these savings accrued more to higher-traffic, longer-distance routes than to shorter ones.

possibility_chains: A low-cost carrier entering a new route or market has historically forced incumbent legacy carriers to cut their own fares on that route in direct response, rather than cede the market entirely.

Sustained low-cost-carrier competition following deregulation has historically compressed average industry fares over a period of years to decades, with the effect concentrated on the routes most exposed to new low-cost entrants.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: US Airline Deregulation Act and the growth of low-cost, point-to-point carriers (1978–1994): Average US fares per passenger mile fell about 9% between 1979 and 1994, and inflation-adjusted fares fell roughly 30% between 1976 and 1990; a New York-Los Angeles round trip that would have cost an inflation-adjusted $1,442 in 1974 could be purchased for around $268 by 2010, though these savings accrued more to higher-traffic, longer-distance routes than to shorter ones. A low-cost carrier entering a new route or market has historically forced incumbent legacy carriers to cut their own fares on that route in direct response, rather than cede the market entirely.

linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: American Airlines merges with US Airways (February–December 2013): The merger created what became, by some measurements, the largest airline in the world by passengers carried and scheduled passenger-kilometers flown, completing a consolidation wave that also included United Airlines' 2010 merger with Continental — leaving the US domestic market dominated by four major carriers (American, Delta, United, and Southwest). A period of sustained high fuel costs or post-recession financial stress has historically accelerated airline merger activity, as weaker carriers sought scale and stronger balance sheets through consolidation rather than standalone survival.

About 21,000 Thomas Cook employees worldwide lost their jobs, including 9,000 in the UK; the company had reported a £1.5 billion loss for the first half of 2019, including £1.1 billion in goodwill write-downs. A major tour operator or airline's sudden collapse has historically stranded large numbers of travelers simultaneously, forcing government-coordinated emergency repatriation using capacity chartered from competing airlines.

ripple_effect.name: Fuel subsidy removal triggers public unrest

historical_precedents.what_happened: The government removed Nigeria's longstanding petrol subsidy on January 1, 2012, roughly doubling pump prices from 65 to at least 141 naira per litre; nationwide strikes and protests followed for nearly two weeks (January 2–14) across Lagos, Abuja, Kano, and other cities, with trade unions announcing an indefinite strike from January 9.
historical_precedents.market_impact: About 16 people were killed in clashes between protesters and police, and the government partially walked back the increase before the standoff ended.

historical_precedents.event: Ecuador's Decree 883 fuel subsidy removal and reversal
historical_precedents.what_happened: President Lenín Moreno eliminated 40-year-old fuel subsidies on October 1, 2019 as part of an IMF-linked austerity package addressing $64 billion in debt, roughly doubling diesel prices and raising petrol prices about 30%; indigenous groups (CONAIE), transport workers, and students staged nationwide protests from October 3–14.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The unrest left 8 dead, over 1,300 injured, and nearly 1,200 detained; President Moreno reversed the policy by signing Decree 894 on October 14, 2019, restoring subsidies to previous levels after a televised agreement with indigenous leaders.

possibility_chains: Sudden, large fuel subsidy removals (rather than gradual phase-outs) have historically triggered the fastest and largest public backlash, since the price change is immediate and highly visible to every driver and transport-dependent business at once.

Fuel subsidy cuts tied explicitly to IMF or multilateral lender conditions have historically been politically riskier for a government to sustain than domestically-initiated cuts, since opponents can frame the policy as externally imposed.

Governments facing sustained fuel-subsidy protests have historically had to choose between accepting significant political and fiscal cost from unrest or reversing the policy and returning to the fiscal drain the subsidy represented — full reversal has been a common outcome even after violent confrontations.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: Ecuador's Decree 883 fuel subsidy removal and reversal (October 2019): The unrest left 8 dead, over 1,300 injured, and nearly 1,200 detained; President Moreno reversed the policy by signing Decree 894 on October 14, 2019, restoring subsidies to previous levels after a televised agreement with indigenous leaders. Sudden, large fuel subsidy removals (rather than gradual phase-outs) have historically triggered the fastest and largest public backlash, since the price change is immediate and highly visible to every driver and transport-dependent business at once.

Shipping insurers have historically raised war-risk premiums for vessels transiting the Gulf during periods of heightened tension, adding to the landed cost of oil and other cargo.

historical_precedents.market_impact: A 'grand bargain' brokered by the presiding judge had private foundations commit $366 million over 20 years to protect pensions and keep the Detroit Institute of Arts' collection out of a creditor sale, reducing pension cuts from a proposed 50% to about 4.5%; the city exited bankruptcy within 17 months, and contrary to fears of wider contagion, investors subsequently treated other cities' general obligation bonds as relatively safe.

historical_precedents.what_happened: Jefferson County filed for what was then the largest US municipal bankruptcy on November 9, 2011, with $4.2 billion in debt, $3.14 billion of it tied to a sewer system overhaul whose costs spiraled after county officials entered risky interest-rate swap agreements arranged amid bribery; six former county commissioners and 15 other officials were ultimately convicted of corruption.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The county cut its government workforce by more than 700 employees by May 2012, and the bankruptcy court wrote off more than $1.4 billion of the debt before the county emerged from bankruptcy in December 2013.

ripple_effect.name: Persian Gulf oil supply shock

historical_precedents.what_happened: Iran and Iraq attacked oil tankers transiting the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz, and Iran repeatedly threatened to close the strait.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Shipping insurance war-risk premiums in the Gulf rose sharply, and the U.S. Navy began escorting reflagged Kuwaiti tankers in 1987 to keep the strait open.

historical_precedents.event: Drone and missile attack on Saudi Aramco's Abqaiq and Khurais facilities
historical_precedents.what_happened: The attack (which Saudi Arabia and the U.S. blamed on Iran, a claim Iran denied) temporarily knocked out roughly half of Saudi Arabia's oil output, about 5% of global supply.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Brent crude jumped about 15% in a single day — the largest one-day oil price increase since the 1990–91 Gulf War.

historical_precedents.what_happened: Iraq's invasion of Kuwait removed a large share of Gulf oil exports from the market and raised fears of a wider regional war.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Oil prices roughly doubled in the months following the invasion before falling back once the war ended and supply concerns eased.

possibility_chains: Roughly a fifth of the world's oil is estimated to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, so a sustained blockage or major disruption there has historically driven crude oil prices sharply higher.

Because ammonia-based fertilizer production is natural-gas intensive, and natural gas prices often move together with oil, a prolonged energy price spike has historically fed through into higher fertilizer costs over the following months.
Fertilizer is a major input cost in food production, so energy shocks of this kind have historically been followed — often with a lag — by higher food prices.
Shipping insurers have historically raised war-risk premiums for vessels transiting the Gulf during periods of heightened tension, adding to the landed cost of oil and other cargo.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: Gulf War (Iraqi invasion of Kuwait) (1990–1991): Oil prices roughly doubled in the months following the invasion before falling back once the war ended and supply concerns eased. Roughly a fifth of the world's oil is estimated to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, so a sustained blockage or major disruption there has historically driven crude oil prices sharply higher.

signals.headline: ‘We Don’t Need Canada’: Trump Escalates Trade War With Threat of 50% Auto Tariffs

ripple_effect.name: Major tariff escalation / trade war

historical_precedents.what_happened: The U.S. imposed tariffs on hundreds of billions of dollars of Chinese goods, and China retaliated with its own tariffs, including on U.S. agricultural exports.
historical_precedents.market_impact: U.S. soybean exports to China fell sharply, and the U.S. government paid out tens of billions of dollars in subsidies to farmers hurt by the retaliation; global manufacturers reported higher input costs and supply-chain uncertainty through the period.

historical_precedents.what_happened: The U.S. raised tariffs on over 20,000 imported goods to some of the highest levels in a century; Canada, France, and other major trading partners retaliated with their own tariffs within months.
historical_precedents.market_impact: World trade volumes fell by roughly two-thirds over the following four years; widely cited by economists as having deepened and prolonged the Great Depression globally, not just in the U.S. — the clearest historical example that a major tariff escalation's damage isn't confined to the two countries directly involved.

historical_precedents.event: China's rare earth export restrictions on Japan
historical_precedents.what_happened: After Japan detained a Chinese trawler captain following a collision near the disputed Senkaku/Diaoyu Islands, China informally slowed rare earth mineral shipments to Japan without declaring a formal ban.
historical_precedents.market_impact: China's rare earth exports fell roughly 77% year-on-year by September 2011, and global prices spiked several-fold (cerium oxide rose from around $4.70/kg in April 2010 to around $36/kg that October). The U.S. filed a WTO case in 2012; the WTO ruled against China in 2014, and China dropped its export quotas in 2015 — but the episode had already pushed Japan and other importers to diversify sourcing and boost recycling.

Extended periods of tariff uncertainty have historically led some companies to shift or diversify supply chains toward other countries, a process that has typically played out over one to several years, not weeks.

historical_precedents.market_impact: The World Bank estimated the outbreak cost the three hardest-hit countries over $2 billion in lost economic output.

historical_precedents.what_happened: The WHO declared a Public Health Emergency as Zika spread across the Americas, linked to birth defects; several countries issued travel advisories affecting tourism, notably ahead of the Rio de Janeiro Olympics.

Vaccine and treatment developers have historically seen increased investment and expedited regulatory review during major outbreaks.

signals.headline: Rentrée-scolaire : Comment surmonter les difficultés financières et sécuritaires ?

ripple_effect.name: Teacher strike wave

historical_precedents.what_happened: About 20,000 West Virginia teachers and school personnel struck for nine school days across all 55 counties, closing schools for roughly 250,000 students, after rejecting a 2% pay offer amid the state ranking 48th nationally in teacher pay and facing rising health-insurance costs; rank-and-file teachers turned it into a wildcat strike by refusing a union-leadership back-to-work order partway through.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The strike ended with a 5% pay raise for all state employees, and — more significantly for the labor-market ripple — directly inspired similarly organized "Red for Ed" teacher strikes and walkouts in Oklahoma, Colorado, Arizona, and smaller actions in North Carolina and Kentucky later the same year, spreading a strike tactic across states with no formal teachers'-union relationship to West Virginia's.

possibility_chains: A successful teacher strike win in one state has historically been cited explicitly by organizers in other states within the same school year, spreading the tactic geographically faster than typical multi-year union organizing cycles.

Multi-day school closures from teacher strikes have historically forced working parents to arrange alternative childcare or miss work themselves, a secondary economic cost that rarely shows up in strike-cost estimates focused only on the education sector.

State legislatures facing a high-profile teacher strike have historically faced pressure to address teacher pay and school funding in the same budget cycle, beyond just the immediate strike settlement.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: 2018 West Virginia teachers' strike (22 February – 7 March 2018): The strike ended with a 5% pay raise for all state employees, and — more significantly for the labor-market ripple — directly inspired similarly organized "Red for Ed" teacher strikes and walkouts in Oklahoma, Colorado, Arizona, and smaller actions in North Carolina and Kentucky later the same year, spreading a strike tactic across states with no formal teachers'-union relationship to West Virginia's. A successful teacher strike win in one state has historically been cited explicitly by organizers in other states within the same school year, spreading the tactic geographically faster than typical multi-year union organizing cycles.

linked_playbooks.name: Large-scale healthcare worker strike
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: NHS pay disputes and strikes, United Kingdom (2022–2024): The strikes forced the cancellation or postponement of large numbers of scheduled NHS appointments, procedures, and surgeries during each strike day, adding to an already elevated NHS treatment backlog inherited from the pandemic. A large healthcare-worker strike has historically forced hospitals to postpone non-emergency procedures and appointments for its duration, extending existing treatment backlogs rather than simply pausing them.

linked_playbooks.name: Broad-based voluntary quits wave / labor shortage
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: The "Great Resignation" in the United States (March 2021 – mid-2023): Employers responded with the fastest wage growth in two decades — 4.5% year-over-year in December 2021 — while hospitality, healthcare, and education faced acute staffing shortages that pushed many businesses to accelerate investment in automation and self-service technology; quits rates did not return to pre-pandemic 2019 norms until mid-2023. A sustained period of unusually high voluntary quits has historically coincided with faster wage growth, as employers compete harder to retain and attract staff in a tight labor market.
